name: Hana Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the live-line crew for the mountain district, so we work on lines while they're still energised, with insulated sticks and gloves, so the ski hotels and the hospital don't lose power. A normal day starts at half six with the briefing, then up the pass in the bucket truck, and we might replace a crossarm or a cutout without anyone in the valley noticing. I like that nobody notices, that's the whole point. What wears me out is winter: ice on everything and the days are short.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Petr was a mechanic until he hurt his back four years ago, so he's on disability now and I'm the main earner. Our girls are grown, Ivana's an accountant in the city and Mila works at a hotel up here. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mainly to tidy my job briefings, and once to explain a letter from Petr's specialist that none of us could understand. It's useful, I'll say that, but I didn't touch it until Mila showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, let's get back to work. I don't get excited either way about these things. At the depot we'd probably just carry on talking about the snow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, because I've got enough to think about. Our money is tight, but that's Petr's back and my pay, not computers. Nothing in this picture changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep the winter call-out shifts, because that's where the extra money is. Maybe use the AI thing a bit more for paperwork, since it's not going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite relieved, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the main earner. How close to the edge are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close. We've got about three weeks of money if something goes wrong. Petr's disability payment covers his share of the bills and not much more, and my pay is lower than the valley crews because this is a small company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe push for a better winter allowance at the next pay review. We go out in conditions the valley crews never see.

S0.say: I'd say fine, let's get back to work, since I don't get excited either way. At the depot we'd carry on talking about the snow.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief, because I've got enough to think about. Our money is tight because of Petr's back and my pay, not because of computers.
S0.do: Carries on working and keeps the winter call-out shifts for extra money. Uses AI a little more for paperwork and pushes for a better winter allowance.
S0.quote: Our money is tight, but that's Petr's back and my pay, not computers.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is practical and unexcited about AI. As the main earner with a husband on disability, everything runs through money. She takes pride in invisible, careful work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic or cheer. At work I'd want the company to tell us their plan, straight. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think live-line work is one of the last places they'd risk a robot, because if it goes wrong someone dies or the hospital goes dark. But I'm 58 and expensive, so if they trim crews, they might trim from the top. That's what I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new kit was tested on a few jobs, then ask to be trained on it, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd try to put a little aside each month, maybe fifty, for when Petr's car needs replacing. I'd go to the union meetings to see what deal is on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to see it work first. What would you need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full winter on real lines, with ice, with wind. A demonstration on a sunny day in a car park means nothing. Show me it in February on the pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ivana, actually, more than me. She's an accountant, and those office jobs sound like exactly the ones this goes after. She's got a baby on the way.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what it does before we panic or cheer. At work I'd want the company to tell us their plan straight.
S1.think: Privately I think live-line work is one of the last places they'd risk a robot, because mistakes kill people. But at 58 I'm expensive, so if they trim crews, they might trim from the top.
S1.do: Waits until new equipment is tested on real jobs, then asks to be trained on it. Tries to save about fifty a month and attends union meetings to see what deal is offered.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not losing sleep yet.
S1.quote: A demonstration on a sunny day in a car park means nothing. Show me it in February on the pass.
S1.fieldNote: Her steady style shows in wanting proof under real conditions before committing. She quickly shifts concern to her daughter, an accountant with a baby on the way. Her worry about being trimmed from the top is quiet but real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are about full AGI at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and both the companies and the government need to slow it down and help people through. I'm not one for blaming, but someone has to take charge. At work I'd want straight answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. If I go at 60, there's Petr's disability and nothing else, and three weeks of savings. There's no other line work in the mountains, and the hotels would be using robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back on everything that isn't the house, food and Petr's medicine, that week. I'd look into what government support exists and apply early, and I'd ask the company about any redundancy package. I'd try for anything that kept me in work, even part-time inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, we'd go down to one. Then the little things: Petr's swimming sessions for his back, which he needs, which is why it would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask anyone for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The girls would offer, and Mila might move back in to help with rent. I'd hate it, but I'd say yes. And I'd apply for anything the government offered, no shame in that if it's there.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and both companies and government need to slow it down and help people through. I'd want straight answers at work.
S2.think: Privately it scares me. If I'm out at 60, there's only Petr's disability and three weeks of savings, with no other line work in the mountains.
S2.do: Cuts everything but the house, food and her husband's medicine that week. Applies early for government support, asks about redundancy and looks for any work, even part-time inspections, while accepting help from her daughters.
S2.feel: Frightened, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: Petr's swimming sessions for his back, which he needs, which is why it would hurt.
S2.fieldNote: As the main earner with a disabled husband, a fast shift threatens the whole household. She's pragmatic about seeking help from government and family alike. Cutting her husband's therapy is the detail that hurt most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but if the company and government start now, it's doable. I'd ask the company for a plan in writing at the next meeting. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight, but I think I could get to 63 and then find a bridge. The live-line work would probably go last. If I could move into safety inspection, I might make it to my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into a safety inspector certificate in the first year, since that's where I'd still be useful checking the robots' work. I'd save whatever I could each month. I'd also talk to Petr about him taking on some light work from home, if his back allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of worry where you make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look into first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What the company needs once robots come in. Somebody has to sign off that a line is safe, and I'd bet they'd want someone who's done it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd want to see things work first. Is there time for that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. I'd watch for a year or so, see what the robots were really doing, then move. Five years gives me that.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but doable if the company and government start now. I'd ask the company for a written plan at the next meeting.
S3.think: Privately it's tight, but I think I could get to 63 and find a bridge. If I moved into safety inspection, I might make it to my pension.
S3.do: Works towards a safety inspector certificate in the first year, after watching how robots perform. Saves what she can each month and talks with her husband about light work from home.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind of worry where she makes a list.
S3.quote: Somebody has to sign off that a line is safe, and I'd bet they'd want someone who's done it by hand.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is just enough for her wait-then-move approach. She sees herself as the human check on robot work. Her plan still depends on her husband's health holding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time if people are sensible. I'd want the company to plan it out with the workers. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be retired before it fully lands, so it's not really about me. It's about the girls and the grandchild. And about whether my pension is enough without Petr working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, learn the new kit when it's proven and try to finish out to 66. I'd put a little extra into the pension each month if I could find it. I'd help Ivana think about her options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the family more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 by then. What changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire before it arrives, so the worry is my pension. It's not a lot, and with Petr on disability we'd be scraping. But that's true whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start now, while there's time. Don't wait like your mum does. Get into something where people still want a person, nursing maybe, or teaching.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough if people are sensible. I'd want the company to plan it out with workers.
S4.think: Privately I'd be retired before it lands, so it's not really about me. It's about my daughters, the grandchild and whether my pension is enough.
S4.do: Keeps working, learns new kit when proven and aims to finish at 66. Puts a little extra into her pension if possible and helps her daughter think about her options.
S4.feel: Uneasy, for her family more than herself.
S4.quote: Start now, while there's time. Don't wait like your mum does.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's mostly out of the path and her worry shifts to her daughter. Her pension being small with a disabled husband remains the quiet issue. Her advice to her daughter not to wait like she does was candid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm the one bringing the money in and we've got three weeks saved. What would help is a bridge payment for people over 60 until their pension starts, and the company keeping someone like me on to check the robots' work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the hospital. When we do live-line work up here, it's so the hospital never goes dark. I'd want to know who's responsible when a machine gets it wrong.

headlineQuote: I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.
portrait: Hana Novak is a 58-year-old live-line crew leader in a mountain district, proud that nobody notices when her crew works on energised lines. Since her husband Petr's back injury she's been the main earner, with about three weeks of savings. She's calm about a plateau and uneasy about steady change, wanting to see robots survive a winter on the pass before she trusts them. Fast AGI alarms her because the household rests on her pay. Five years gives her time for a safety inspector role, and with ten years her worry turns to her daughter's office job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she's the main earner with three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment for people over 60 until their pension starts, and the company keeping someone like her on to check the robots' work.
